resolutions.rationale: The quoted sentence makes the desert inference intelligible in isolation, but Dennett’s live reply says the passage immediately rejects the analogy, leaving Sapolsky’s inference dependent on incomplete context.
Sapolsky supplies a specific live quotation, but the surrounding book context is disputed by Dennett and neither speaker’s textual account is independently verified in the locked source.

The move engages the pro account of developed control, yet Dennett’s formal reply says the cited passage itself calls the runner framing misleading, so the challenge answers a materially weaker reconstruction.
Whether caused capacities can ground desert is central to the con burden, but the partial quotation does not securely show that Dennett adopts the specific desert position being attacked.
Sapolsky clearly separates Dennett’s quoted sentence from his own interpretation, but presents the moral implication more decisively than the disputed and incomplete textual context supports.

The quotation gives Sapolsky a concrete basis for concern, but inferring magical control and settled desert from a passage Dennett says immediately rejects is materially uncharitable without making either book claim verified fact.

The general case against intuition is relevant, but Dennett’s live reply distinguishes noting that an intuition is met from endorsing the two-stage model, so the move only partly answers his actual position.
Sapolsky reasonably argues that intuitions can mislead, yet he treats the two-stage model as Dennett’s endorsed support even though Dennett’s formal reply expressly reports rejecting that model.

The central distinction between deterministic causation and uncontrollable variation is coherent, but Dennett’s shift from saying freedom depends on randomness to denying coin-flip randomness creates a real internal tension.

Natural selection and deterministic chaos support the limited claim that variation need not be indeterministic, while the move gives little warrant for the further bridge from generated variation to responsible agency.

The reply directly blocks the claim that deterministic causation prevents option generation, but it does not answer Sapolsky’s deeper challenge that the chooser and ranking values have unchosen origins.
Showing that deterministic evolution can generate usable variation materially advances compatibility, but it does not complete the pro burden of explaining why a causally formed chooser is free.

Dennett’s sequence first says freedom depends on randomness, then says coin flips are not random, and then invokes uncontrollable variation, leaving the key terminology materially unstable despite a recoverable core.
Dennett properly limits his conclusion to denying that natural selection proves indeterminism, but his opening statement that freedom depends on randomness is broader and less carefully qualified.
The locked moves already cover compatibilist freedom, reasons-responsive control, evolved capacity, exceptions, and humane sanctions, so no distinct debate-wide pro consequence remains unscored.

The locked moves already cover originating control, continuous causal history, biological self-control, actual choosing, and humane nonblame, so no distinct debate-wide con consequence remains unscored.
